articles.title: The social fallout of working alongside an office workaholic
articles.summary: When employees work alongside a workaholic, they often feel pressured to match those long hours. A new study reveals that this performance pressure drives coworkers to work harder, but it also increases gossip and badmouthing in the office.

articles.title: Teens with authoritarian parents tend to hold more antisocial beliefs, study finds
articles.summary: Teens whose parents lean on yelling, threats, and punishment without explanation tend to hold stronger beliefs that rule-breaking and aggression are acceptable, a four-wave study of U.S. families suggests.

articles.title: Formerly religious individuals exhibit the highest levels of left-wing authoritarianism
articles.summary: People who leave their religion often abandon conservative beliefs but retain an authoritarian mindset. A new study reveals that formerly religious individuals exhibit the highest levels of left-wing authoritarianism, shifting their targets while maintaining rigid ideological styles.

articles.title: When a partner won’t apologize, anxiously attached people may hold bigger grudges
articles.summary: Why do some people hold grudges after a fight? A new study suggests that for people who fear rejection, a partner’s refusal to apologize is linked to more grudge-holding, avoidance, and difficulty forgiving.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
articles.summary: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

articles.title: Subtle mood changes in late life may follow early Alzheimer’s brain changes, study suggests
articles.summary: Does brain pathology spark low mood, or the other way around? In older adults without memory problems, buildup of the Alzheimer’s-related protein tau tended to come first, followed by small increases in depressive symptoms.

articles.title: New study identifies daily communication and personal mindset as key predictors of marital sexual activity
articles.summary: Married couples in South Korea report higher rates of sexual inactivity than their American counterparts, according to a large survey. The research highlights how work hours, income, and communication styles relate to intimacy in different cultural environments.

articles.title: What 25,000 conversations with a psychedelic helpline show about who seeks help
articles.summary: Who calls a psychedelic helpline? An analysis of nearly five years of calls and texts found that psilocybin dominated, cannabis showed up often, and most callers whose setting was recorded were going through it alone.

articles.summary: Researchers have identified a unique brain connectivity pattern linked to cocaine use disorder. This biological marker can distinguish patients from healthy individuals and predict whether they will respond to magnetic brain stimulation therapies to reduce cravings.

articles.title: Eye-tracking study suggests a simple PowerPoint technique can sharpen students’ focus
articles.summary: Teachers often reveal slide content one piece at a time as they talk. A new eye-tracking study suggests the habit pays off: students found the right information faster, looked at it longer, and scored modestly higher afterward.

articles.title: How the loss of male-dominated industrial jobs pushes communities to the political right
articles.summary: As manufacturing and mining jobs vanish, women are entering the workforce to replace lost income. A new study finds this economic rebalancing creates cultural anxiety and financial strain, driving voters across classes toward conservative politicians.

articles.title: New psychology research challenges a popular explanation for why conspiracy theories cluster together
articles.summary: People who believe one conspiracy theory tend to believe others, and many psychologists point to a general suspicious mindset. But a study of nearly 30,000 people suggests that mindset rarely sits at the center.

articles.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
articles.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

articles.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
articles.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

articles.title: Fatherhood brain changes, AI companions, and a dispute over evolution’s grip on romance: The week in psychology podcasts
articles.summary: How much does our evolutionary past dictate whom we love and how we compete? Across this week's podcast conversations, two psychologists offered sharply different answers. One built an account of human intelligence and male status-seeking around ancestral warfare, while another argued that the popular evolutionary script about mate preferences falls apart once people actually meet face to face.
